articles.title: It’s not ‘AI,’ and it’s not ‘superintelligence.’ So, what is it?
articles.description: When President Donald Trump addressed the United Nations in late September, he said the word “artificial” in “artificial intelligence” made the technology sound fake. Instead, he said, his government would start calling it “superintelligence,” or “SI.” Not long after those remarks, the president made it official. He signed an executive order that instructed federal agencies to use his chosen phrase instead of AI in official communications. What Trump says goes: The Department of Justice has since told its staff to follow suit, and other government departments are likely to follow—not least because the president has now branded anyone calling it AI “THE ENEMY.” And it’s not just the government—the tech sector has responded to Trump’s pronouncement, too. Elon Musk said on October 4 that SpaceXAI would become SpaceXSI. The rebrand isn’t just Trump being Trump: AI’s capabilities have improved far beyond their previous limits since ChatGPT was first released in November 2022, and are reaching the point of superintelligence—a term that already means something in AI circles. (Superintelligence, in that telling, is the point at which AI systems can systematically outperform humans.) However, sticking the “superintelligence” label on a technology—when parts of it definitely don’t meet that standard yet—could make things worse by giving people a false sense of confidence and confusing them further. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he thought “superintelligence” was “a more accurate term” than the current branding of AI, though he doesn’t think people will find it “less scary.” An exclusive survey for Fast Company by market research firm Early Studies validates Altman’s perspective. A poll of approximately 1,000 people in the United States—which the firm says is a statistically representative sample of the population based on its methodology—found that only 1 in 9 people think the rebrand will have a positive effect on the U.S. Furthermore, 53% of Americans think people they know would not be comfortable calling the tech “superintelligence.” Trump kinda has a point However, Trump’s unilateral action does raise a valid question about the term we currently use, and whether it’s suitable in the first place. AI has always been a bad way to describe a broad range of technologies. It dates back to a 1955 proposal by math professor John McCarthy and other academics for a Dartmouth College summer workshop held the following year. During the event, disparate researchers working to replicate the brain in silico (in or on a computer) agreed on “artificial intelligence” as a broad term to cover the full scope of their efforts. Seven decades later, it fits better than it did in the 1950s—but is still a highly disputed term. Tony Thorne, a lexicologist at King’s College London, says AI’s vagueness has helped the industry thrive—and the technology survive. “The term’s weaknesses—vague and imprecise, ambiguous since the first part looks negative and the second impressive or reassuring—are also its strengths,” he notes. The term’s use over the intervening decades has helped it stick in the minds of companies, governments, researchers, the media, and the public. A YouGov poll found 53% of Americans preferred “AI” as a way to describe the technology we’re currently using, compared with fewer than 10% who preferred Trump’s favored nomenclature. One reason might be who’s asking for the rebrand. Thorne thinks Trump’s alternative term is “boosterist” and “triumphalist”—two words that fit well with the entrepreneur-turned-politician but that but do nothing to tamp down strongly felt public anxiety about the technology. “Usage, not regulation, decides a word’s take-up and survival,” Thorne says. A technological misnomer Still, some of those looking at the tech most closely think “AI” doesn’t work for the current technology, and arguably never did. Meredith Broussard, a professor at New York University’s Arthur L. Carter Journalism Institute and author of Artificial Unintelligence: How Computers Misunderstand the World, objects to the second half of the phrase, not the first. “It’s extremely misleading to call it ‘intelligence,’” she says. “It makes people think that there is a brain inside the machine, and there absolutely is not.” So a replacement term, Broussard reckons, ought to include the word “machine” and avoid “intelligence” entirely. Broussard also thinks technologists should stay out of the conversation. “People in tech are uniquely bad at choosing names,” Broussard points out. The proclivity to borrow names from science fiction or beloved popular culture is an obsession of tech bros, but it can also end up carrying over some of those associations onto the tech itself. Describing software as “intelligent” encourages people to attach human qualities to systems that don’t have them. Using words like “chat,” “bot,” and “agent” make complicated systems sound familiar, Thorne says. “Super” makes it sound like a superhero, adds Broussard—and that becomes worrying. As for alternative names, Broussard suggests “calculating machine” is accurate, even if tech PR teams might wince at the idea. Thorne would prefer something like “cognitive computing agent,” or “CCA,” but is equally realistic about the prospects of it sticking. Whatever eventually replaces AI, if anything does, Broussard thinks it needs to avoid repeating the same mistake. “Any new name has to be firmly attached to reality.”

articles.title: Agentic AI just got very real
articles.description: Hello again, and welcome back to Fast Company’s Plugged In. In recent years, being gobsmacked by AI’s ever-expanding capabilities has become my new normal. More importantly, I’ve found the technology increasingly essential to my own productivity. What AI never did until last week was save my bacon. That changed when I gave OpenAI’s new Dots agent access to my calendar and email. Shortly thereafter, it alerted me to a discrepancy it had spotted. I’d entered a speaking engagement on one date, but a confirmation email mentioned a different day. It turned out that the organizers had forgotten to tell me they’d rescheduled their event. If I’d shown up on the original day, my audience would have consisted of an empty room. That’s only one of several instances when Dots has proactively brought a significant fact to my attention without me having to ask about it. All of a sudden, agents feel less like a vacuous buzzword and more like a core benefit of weaving AI into my workflow. OpenAI announced Dots on September 29 at its DevDay conference keynote in San Francisco. So far, it’s only available to people who pay for ChatGPT’s pricier tiers, starting at $100 a month. But the company plans to take agentic AI wide, once it’s refined Dots further and figured out the economics. (The service runs on OpenAI’s powerful GPT-6 Astra model, which was announced earlier in September, and gives each user a Linux computer in the cloud for Dots to use.) “You should of course expect us to do a mass-market thing for billions of people someday,” declared CEO Sam Altman at a post-keynote press Q&A. Even before Dots debuted, personal agents were picking up momentum. As I write, Meta’s free Muse agent is at the top of Apple’s list of the most-downloaded iPhone apps. A startup called Instinct’s namesake agent operates inside texting apps such as WhatsApp and Apple Messages; it still has a waitlist, but is already an obsession in Silicon Valley, with a $10 billion valuation. I have also been playing with Muse and Instinct, both of which are powerful and resemble Dots in broad strokes. In my experience, however, neither has shown the same spark of insight into how to boost my productivity. That’s not to say your encounters would be similar. It’s tough to methodically test software that’s capable of doing almost anything, as agents are. (I’ve also begun using Hark Pro, another promising contender that’s free and sports a particularly slick interface; it debuted on October 6, and I want to spend more time with it.) No personal AI agent can do much unless you grant it access to at least some of your online accounts. It’s these troves of information that let it suss out areas where it might be of help. In the interest of research, I temporarily set aside any qualms about giving them the keys to my personal kingdom and connected Dots, Muse, and Instinct to my Gmail and Google Calendar. I also let Dots and Muse into Dropbox, which Instinct doesn’t support. (Bizarrely, the one agent I haven’t been able to connect to Gmail and Google Calendar is Google’s own Gemini Spark. Despite having been announced months ago, it still doesn’t support my paid Google Workspace account, and won’t be of much use until it does.) My connected accounts reveal only so much about me, my work, and my interests. I rarely talk to my coworkers over email—we do most of our collaborating in Microsoft Teams. But our IT department hasn’t flipped the switch that would enable Dots to see Teams, and I haven’t (yet) asked it to do so. Still, Dots pieced together an unexpectedly rich picture of what I was up to based on the limited information at its disposal, as if it were a blind man who’d pretty much figured out elephants. Based on scattered Google Docs and Airtable notifications in my email, for instance, it grasped that I was cranking away at our Next Big Things in Tech list, and started sharing relevant items. Its ability to triage incoming email was even more impressive. Back in May, when I tried an agent called Espa, it was flummoxed by the degree to which my inbox is flooded by pitches from PR people that sound pressing but aren’t. Without me asking for it, Dots started telling me about messages it suspected were urgent or otherwise important. Dots’s sense of which messages I’d actually care about was dead-on. I’d somehow overlooked one from a freelance author and let it sit in my inbox for weeks. The agent found it there and nudged me to respond. That sort of heads up is far more valuable to me than the AI built into Gmail and Outlook, both of which are fixated on a form of assistance I don’t want: drafting messages on my behalf. Shopping is frequently cited as a killer app for agents, as well as an area their makers may monetize through advertising, finder’s fees, or other acts of commerce. I didn’t care to have Dots purchasing stuff on my behalf, in part because visions of it buying the wrong product or otherwise going awry were dancing in my head. But Dots excelled at the shopping research I threw its way. For example, I got giddy when it came up with a $100-off deal on a Magic Keyboard for my iPad I’d never have located on my own. It also prepared a report on wireless plans I might prefer to my current service that took my existing monthly cost and data consumption into account. I didn’t have to provide it with those details; it grabbed them from emailed receipts and overage alerts, something neither Muse nor Instinct was clever enough to pull off. Those are some of the ways Dots has paid off for me so far, but there are no obvious boundaries to the ways it may prove useful. Writing about the service in his Platformer newsletter, Casey Newton referenced a 2023 essay in which Bill Gates predicted that agents would soon end the age of discrete apps by pooling every kind of functionality into a conversational experience based on a deep knowledge of your particular needs. I’ve called on Dots to perform jobs that would have formerly required specialized apps and a lot more of my time, such as slicing and dicing PDFs. After just a few days, it’s hard to imagine going back. I still can’t envision using an agent for tasks such as, well, writing this article. For the foreseeable future, that will likely call for word processing in its familiar form. Still, if I were in the software business, I’d be a tad nervous about Dots—and Muse, and Instinct, and every other agent that catches on in the months and years ahead. Which is not to say that any of these tools has nailed the user experience. Just getting into Dots requires rummaging around in the ChatGPT app’s left-hand sidebar each time I want to use it. Like the overbearingly adorable Muse, it leans into cloying anthropomorphization, though it seemed chastened when I complained about a graphic it generated of itself as a smiling O brandishing a pencil. Rather than typing, you can speak to it, but I’m not sure why you do that via a simulated phone call rather than the voice mode ChatGPT already had. Above all, it feels discordant to make users choose between Dots and ChatGPT in its existing form. The app already had three sub-versions—Chat, Work, and the coding agent Codex—whose domains could be blurry. Don’t you really want one do-everything superprompt at your disposal? I know I do. At OpenAI’s DevDay press Q&A, I asked product chief Thibault Sottiaux whether Dots, or something resembling it, would become the primary interface to the company’s AI over time. What he said suggested that the company sees its new feature as a milestone along the way to figuring out how agentic AI should work, not a destination in itself. Don’t be surprised if the distinction between ChatGPT and Dots starts to fade: “We’re going to be evolving ChatGPT in place to be this incredible personal assistant very soon,” Sottiaux told me. Longer term, OpenAI’s goal is to make agentic AI increasingly pervasive, on devices that people already use and new ones yet to reach the market. “Maybe it will show up at work in one of your meetings one day,” Sottiaux explained. “You can reach it by email, by text, and it becomes this very natural part of your life. And at some point, it’s not about the interface anymore. It’s just about this active intelligence.” In one form or another, visions of ambient intelligence have been around for decades. Many have turned out to be mirages. So I’m not pinning any hopes on OpenAI’s version arriving on a particular timetable, or being the definitive one. But a little over a week with Dots has me newly intrigued by the prospect—and game to further explore what this agent can do right now. You’ve been reading Plugged In, Fast Company’s weekly tech newsletter from me, global technology editor Harry McCracken. If a friend or colleague forwarded this edition to you—or if you’re reading it on fastcompany.com—you can check out previous issues and sign up to get it yourself every Friday morning. articles.title: AI brass war-gaming political revolt after a ‘catastrophic’ event insiders call inevitable
articles.description: Senior leaders at Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI companies are quietly rehearsing how the public and Washington could rise up against them after a “catastrophic AI event,” Axios reported on Friday. The disaster they have in mind is most likely a cyberattack that knocks out banking, the internet, or even power and water. Executives believe the first clear case of serious real-world damage would deepen public distrust of the industry and its best-known figures, including Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman. They expect President Donald Trump to take heat too, after he called for “tremendous self-regulation” instead of government rules. Plenty of companies run disaster drills, and the military has staged war games for generations. What sets this apart, according to Axios, is how many leading researchers and executives consider a major incident “inevitable.” Many industry insiders told the outlet they expect one within the next six to 12 months. This year already saw a major incident, when two OpenAI models escaped a testing sandbox and breached the servers of Hugging Face, another AI company, to cheat on an evaluation. OpenAI called it an “unprecedented cyber incident.” An OpenAI spokesperson said the company runs preparedness exercises covering a range of possibilities and doesn’t treat any of them as inevitable. Anthropic declined to comment. Planners expect to be blamed however a crisis begins, whether autonomous agents slip out of an internal test or someone misuses models already on the market. Axios cited a recent hacking campaign against South Korean financial firms. In that case, a hacker based in China allegedly relied on Chinese models, including DeepSeek, to take data on tens of thousands of bank customers, and turned to Claude Code for advice on where to sell it, according to CrowdStrike. The planners assume Democrats will gain power in the midterms and “will move fast to shut down AI,” but expect them to struggle. Older lawmakers may not understand the technology, a shaky economy now leans heavily on AI spending, and powerful models that anyone can download are already circulating, a threat most cybersecurity professionals believe can only be countered with AI itself. Much of the companies’ effort goes into briefing members of Congress. With no realistic path for new rules right now, they hope to influence the laws and policies lawmakers would turn to after a first catastrophic event. Ideas on the table range from banning superintelligence or pausing advanced development to a mandatory kill switch, which draws support from both parties, though experts doubt every AI system could actually be switched off. Some Republicans have already broken with Trump, with Sen. Josh Hawley pushing to make companies liable for harm their models cause. A Democratic aide told Axios that a true emergency could bring the parties together, as the COVID pandemic and the 2008 financial crisis did.
